content:
Local weather is one of the most underrated variables in Apple Home smart home automation setups. Over the past few years, I've used various sensors for everything from when to drip faucets during freezing weather to adjusting sprinkler timing on hot days with the Eve Aqua. The Eve Weather has been in my setup for a while now, and since it gained Matter support a few years ago, it has really served me well at home.

HomeKit Weekly is a column series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything related to Apple's smart home framework.

If you've been following HomeKit Weekly for a while, you know I'm a big fan of automation that runs on its own. The value of smart home accessories lies in what they can do automatically. That's why I've always recommended building your smart home around a single ecosystem rather than mixing and matching brands from all over. Even in the age of Matter, I don't want to juggle a bunch of different platforms. For me, that platform is Apple Home. I prefer Eve's devices because they've always taken privacy seriously, and as long as you stick with local control over Matter, you don't need to open a cloud account. Eve has been very proactive in supporting Matter and Thread in recent years. This is exactly what you want to see.

The Eve Weather gives you three sets of data in one compact device: temperature, humidity, and barometric pressure. It carries an IPX4 water resistance rating and features an aluminum housing that fits in perfectly outdoors. Mine is mounted right outside. It delivers highly accurate local readings that are often several degrees off from what the Apple Weather app reports. Honestly, that few-degree difference really matters during extreme cold or heat. When your pipes are freezing at 31 degrees Fahrenheit, but the app says 34 degrees, you'll regret not paying attention to local data.

One of the Eve Weather's most underrated features is its built-in 12-hour weather trend display. It uses barometric pressure changes to predict weather trends. You'll see a visual icon indicating whether it's likely to be sunny, cloudy, rainy, or stormy. This small detail brings considerable practical value—you can see it at a glance without having to open a phone app.

Here are a few examples of automations you can set up with the Eve Weather:

  • When temperatures drop below freezing, turn on a colored light to remind family members to drip the faucets.
  • When outdoor humidity is particularly high, activate the dehumidifier.
  • If it's already rained and the forecast shows more rain coming, delay the sprinkler system.
  • Ask Siri from indoors what the temperature is in the front yard right now.

Matter and Thread support in 2026

A few years ago, Eve released a free firmware update that added Matter support to the Eve Weather. If you already own the device, you can upgrade through the Eve app. The Matter version supports Apple Home as well as Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and SmartThings. The sensor itself remains identical—just now cross-platform compatible, so even if you want to switch to a different primary smart home ecosystem in the future, you won't have to replace the device.

The Eve Weather falls into a category called a "Minimal Thread Device." That means it communicates via Thread but doesn't relay traffic. That job is left to always-on "Full Thread Devices" such as the Eve Energy or Eve Water Guard. The more Full Thread Devices you have, the stronger and more stable your Thread network becomes, and battery-powered devices like the Eve Weather directly benefit from that stability.

You still don't need to create an Eve account. Unless you choose to, everything stays handled locally. The Eve iPhone app is an excellent tool for visualizing and logging historical temperature, barometric pressure, and humidity trends. It's really a great way to spot patterns and make smarter decisions about things like lawn watering and energy management.

I have several HomePod minis around the house, and I also rely on my Eero 6E network to support Thread. Eero has Thread support built into its software, so it provides a solid foundation for accessories like the Eve Weather, keeping them connected and running quickly.

Eve Weather Summary

The only improvement I still really want to see is a rechargeable battery. The current battery life lasts several months, but I'd much prefer a USB-C port like the Eve Room has. Apart from that, the Eve Weather is one of my favorite Apple Home accessories. It's simple, good-looking, and works well across all major platforms, thanks to Matter. If you want to add local weather information to your smart home along with practical automations, the Eve Weather is a no-brainer recommendation from me.

You can buy it on Amazon or directly from the Eve Store.
